E052-01.notes: Object of preposition 'of' in a relative clause needs 'whom': 'Skaters, many of whom had paid...'. A 'who' is subject case. B 'many of them had paid' makes an independent clause spliced into the sentence ('Skaters, many of them had paid for a full evening, spent...' has two finite verbs with no connector). D 'many of whose had paid' is ungrammatical (whose needs a following noun).

E052-02.notes: 'Spending most of the 1940s on the problem' is a participial phrase, not a sentence; attach it with a comma: 'decided to build a machine that could do the job alone, spending most of the 1940s on the problem.' A leaves a fragment. B semicolon requires an independent clause after it; the participial phrase is not one. C 'and spending' has no parallel verb to join to ('decided ... and spending' mismatches forms), leaving a dangling coordinate.

E052-03.notes: 'His first successful model' is already uniquely identified, so 'which he finished in 1949' is nonessential and needs a pair of commas: 'His first successful model, which he finished in 1949, combined three tasks.' A omits both commas (and 'which' signals nonrestrictive). C opens the clause but never closes it, so the clause runs into the main verb. D places a lone comma between subject and verb.

E052-04.notes: A colon after the complete clause 'combined three tasks' correctly introduces the list. B semicolon needs an independent clause after it; the list is not one. C 'such as:' puts a colon after 'such as' (incorrect) and 'such as' implies a partial set of examples, contradicting 'three tasks' with exactly three listed. D 'three tasks that were shaving the ice, washing it, and drying it' is wordy and awkward, and turns the tasks into a progressive-verb construction.

E052-05.notes: C gives concrete contrast (one driver vs. a crew; minutes vs. more than an hour), directly echoing sentence 3 and showing reduced work. A 'faster' is vague and says nothing about the labor. B 'clear improvement' is generic. D addresses where it worked, not how much work it saved.

flags.note: 'the company's' has no antecedent; the passage never mentions that Zamboni founded a company (sentences 8-9 speak only of the machine and orders). Consider adding a brief mention of the company or rewording to 'Zamboni's later models'.

E052-06.notes: Subject is singular 'Each', so 'Each of the company's later models was smaller and quicker.' A and C use plural 'were' (C also adds a comma between subject and verb). D 'have been' is plural and also shifts tense away from the past narrative.

E052-07.notes: 'regardless of who made it' clarifies that people call any resurfacer a Zamboni even when another maker built it. A: nothing about naming models. B: the phrase does not claim superiority. C: nothing about the company stopping production.

E052-08.notes: 'the figure skater Sonja Henie' is a restrictive appositive (the name identifies which figure skater), so no commas: 'the figure skater Sonja Henie saw the machine'. B sets off the name as nonessential, making the sentence read as if only one figure skater exists. C puts a single comma between 'skater' and the name and none after, leaving the appositive half-punctuated. D a lone dash with no closing dash is incorrect and unwarranted.

E052-09.notes: Sentence 9 ('Within a few years, rinks across the country were placing orders') follows naturally from Henie's 1950 order in sentence 8 and leads into later models in 10. B before 8 puts the spread ahead of its first famous buyer, and 'Within a few years' would lack a reference point (it would follow the 1949 model paragraph break oddly). C after 10 interrupts the sequence between later models and the closing note on the name. D after 11 tacks a chronological detail onto the 'Today' conclusion.
